# Brainstem

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Basics of neurology > Brainstem*

[Original Article Link](/library/b70H4h)

---

## Summary

The brainstem is the <u>caudal</u> part of the <u>brain</u> and consists of the <u>midbrain</u>, <u>pons</u>, and <u>medulla oblongata</u>. The brainstem regulates autonomic functions (respiration, circulation, <u>lacrimation</u>, salivation), controls visual and auditory reflexes, and maintains vigilance. It is also a hub through which run all ascending <u>sensory pathways</u>, descending <u>motor pathways</u>, and other local pathways of the <u>central nervous system</u>.

---

## Overview

### <u>Embryogenesis</u>




* <u>Mesencephalon</u> → <u>midbrain</u>

* <u>Rhombencephalon</u>

* <u>Metencephalon</u> → <u>pons</u> and <u>cerebellum</u>

* <u>Myelencephalon</u> → <u>medulla oblongata</u>





![Regions of the brain with embryological derivation](media/szgnm1qphhtm92novs0i774n.jpg)

Regions of the brain with embryological derivation




### Composition




* Parts (superior to inferior):

* <u>Midbrain</u>

* <u>Pons</u>

* <u>Medulla oblongata</u>

* <u>Nuclei</u> of <u>CN III</u>–XII

* Major ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) pathways

* Reticular formation (responsible for alertness)

| <br>Rule 2: Four factors of 12 except 1 and 2 are purely motor <u>nuclei</u> (<u>CN III</u>, IV, VI and XII). To localize brainstem <u>strokes</u>, remember the four rules of four.  Rule 1: Four <u>nuclei</u> are below the <u>pons</u> (<u>CN IX</u>–XII in the medulla), four are in the <u>pons</u> (<u>CN V</u>–VIII), and four are above the <u>pons</u> (<u>CN III</u> and IV in the <u>midbrain</u>, <u>CN I</u> and II originate from the <u>cerebrum</u>). Rule 3: Four structures beginning with M are located in the middle: purely Motor <u>nuclei</u>, Motor pathway (<u>corticospinal tract</u>), Medial lemniscus (<u>proprioception</u> and vibration in the trunk and extremities), and Medial longitudinal fasciculus (coordinating <u>eye movements</u>). Rule 4: Four structures beginning with S are located to the side: Spinocerebellar pathway, Spinothalamic tract (<u>pain</u> and temperature in the trunk and extremities), Spinal sensory <u>nucleus</u> of <u>CN V</u> (<u>pain</u> and <u>temperature sensation</u> in the face), and Sympathetic pathway.<br> |  |  |

### Function




* Regulation of awareness and <u>sleep cycle</u>

* Regulation of autonomic functions (e.g., circulation, respiration, gastrointestinal activity, salivation, <u>lacrimation</u>)

* Conduction

* Ascending <u>sensory tracts</u> via <u>cranial nerves</u> (face) and spinal cord (rest of the body)

* Descending <u>motor tracts</u> from forebrain and <u>cerebellum</u> to neck and face (via <u>cranial nerves</u>) and the rest of the body (via spinal cord)

* Local pathways (e.g., visual and auditory reflexes)

## Midbrain

### Characteristics




* Location: <u>rostral</u> to the <u>pons</u>, <u>ventral</u> to the <u>cerebellum</u>, <u>caudal</u> to the <u>thalamus</u>

* Function

* Processing of auditory and visual information

* Coordination of <u>eye</u> movement

* Modulation of extrapyramidal <u>motor function</u>

* Conduction of fiber tracts

* <u>Nociception</u>

* Arousal and alertness

* Composition: three main components

* <u>Crura cerebri</u>

* <u>Tegmentum</u>

* <u>Tectum</u>

* <u>Embryogenesis</u>: derived from <u>mesencephalon</u>





### Components of the midbrain




| Overview of the <u>midbrain</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Location | Components | Function/Characteristics |
| <br>Tectum  <br> | <br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> to the <u>cerebral aqueduct</u><br><br>* Forms the roof of the <u>midbrain</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Superior colliculi<br><br> | <br><br>* Relay voluntary and involuntary <u>eye movements</u> (e.g., <u>saccades</u>)<br><br>* Facilitate optic reflexes<br><br>* Receive input from the <u>retina</u> and the <u>pretectal area</u><br><br>* Project to the <u>lateral geniculate bodies</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>* Inferior colliculi<br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>auditory pathway</u><br><br>* Receive input from the <u>lateral lemniscus</u><br><br>* Project to the <u>medial geniculate bodies</u><br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>Tegmentum  <br> | <br><br>* Extends from <u>midbrain</u> to <u>pons</u><br><br>* Between the <u>tectum</u> and the base of the <u>midbrain</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Sensory pathways</u> and <u>nuclei</u> of <u>oculomotor nerve</u> (<u>CN III</u>) and <u>trochlear nerve</u> (<u>CN IV</u>)<br><br>* <u>Mesencephalic</u> <u>nucleus</u> of <u>trigeminal nerve</u> (<u>CN V</u>)<br><br>* <u>Substantia nigra</u> (see below)<br><br>* <u>Red nucleus</u> (see below)<br><br><br> | <br>* Involved in modulation of extrapyramidal <u>motor function</u><br><br> |
| <br>Substantia nigra  <br> | <br>* Within the <u>tegmentum</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Pars compacta: contains <u>dopaminergic</u> <u>neurons</u> with high levels of <u>melanin</u><br><br>* Pars reticularis: contains mainly <u>GABAergic</u> <u>neurons</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Involved in initiating and coordinating movements<br><br>* Receives inhibitory input (<u>GABA</u>) from the <u>striatum</u><br><br>* Projects <u>dopaminergic</u> fibers to the <u>striatum</u> (↑ motor function)<br><br>* Projects <u>GABAergic</u> fibers to motoric <u>nuclei</u> (e.g., <u>ventral</u> <u>lateral</u>, <u>ventral</u> <u>anterior</u>) of the <u>thalamus</u> (↓ motor function)<br><br>* For more information on the <u>basal ganglia</u>, see also “<u>Basal ganglia</u>” in “<u>The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system</u>.”<br><br>* For information on associated disorders, see “<u>Parkinson disease</u>” and “<u>Parkinson-plus syndromes</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <br>Red nucleus  <br> | <br>* Within the <u>tegmentum</u>, at the level of the <u>oculomotor nerve</u> <u>nucleus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Caudal</u> magnocellular part<br><br>* <u>Rostral</u> parvocellular part<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Coordination of movement and gait<br><br>* Preservation of muscular tone<br><br>* Receives and relays input from the <u>cerebral cortex</u> and the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br>* Origin of the <u>rubrospinal tract</u> and <u>rubroolivary tracts</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Crura cerebri  <br> | <br>* Form the base of the <u>midbrain</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Corticospinal tracts</u><br><br>* <u>Corticopontine tracts</u><br><br>* <u>Corticobulbar tracts</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Voluntary movement of the <u>contralateral</u> side of the body<br><br>* Coordination of planned movement<br><br>* Voluntary movement of muscles of the face and neck<br><br>* For more information on <u>spinal cord tracts</u>, see “<u>Spinal cord tracts and reflexes</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Cerebellar peduncles</u>  <br> | <br>* Arise at the <u>lateral</u> <u>ventral</u> aspect of the <u>pons</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Superior cerebellar peduncles</u><br><br>* <u>Middle cerebellar peduncles</u><br><br>* <u>Inferior cerebellar peduncles</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Relay motor planning signals from the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br>* Relay proprioceptive signals to the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br>* Connection of<br><br>* <u>Pons</u> to <u>cerebellum</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebellum</u> to <u>midbrain</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebellum</u> to medulla and spinal cord<br><br>* For more information on the <u>cerebellar peduncles</u>, see “<u>Cerebellar peduncles</u>” in “<u>Cerebellum</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| Pretectal area (<u>pretectum</u>) | <br><br>* <u>Dorsal</u> side of the <u>midbrain</u> in close proximity to the <u>tectum</u><br><br>* Between <u>thalamus</u> and <u>superior colliculus</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Seven <u>nuclei</u> (e.g., olivary pretectal <u>nucleus</u>, <u>optic tract</u> <u>nucleus</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the subcortical visual system<br><br>* Modulates behavior in reaction to light (e.g., <u>pupillary reflex</u> and <u>accommodation</u>)<br><br>* Receives input from the <u>retina</u> and occipital cortical fields<br><br>* Projects to the <u>Edinger-Westphal nucleus</u> and the <u>superior colliculus</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Cerebral aqueduct</u>  <br> | <br><br>* Between the <u>tegmentum</u> and the <u>tectum</u><br><br>* Surrounded by <u>periaqueductal gray matter</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebrospinal fluid</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Connects the 3<sup>rd</sup> and <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricles</u><br><br>* Stenosis of this structure causes <u>non-communicating hydrocephalus</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Periaqueductal gray matter  <br> | <br>* Surrounds the <u>cerebral aqueduct</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Dorsal</u> tegmental <u>nucleus</u><br><br>* <u>Dorsal</u> <u>raphe nucleus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>antinociceptive system</u><br><br>* <u>Learning</u> of defensive/aversive behavior<br><br>* Response to perceived threat (e.g., increased alertness, initiation of <u>escape</u> actions)<br><br><br> |
| Medial longitudinal fasciculus | <br>* Found on each side near the midline <u>ventral</u> to the <u>fourth ventricle</u> (in the medulla and <u>pons</u>) and <u>cerebral aqueduct</u> (in the <u>midbrain</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>White matter</u> fiber bundles (ascending and descending)<br><br> | <br><br>* Coordinate <u>eye</u> movement<br><br>* Highly myelinated (to enable fast coordinated <u>eye movements</u>)<br><br>* Connect <u>CN III</u>, <u>CN IV</u>, and <u>CN VI</u><br><br>* Lesions lead to <u>internuclear ophthalmoplegia</u><br><br>* Common site of involvement in <u>multiple sclerosis</u> (esp. bilateral lesions)<br><br><br> |
| Central tegmental tract | <br>* From the <u>midbrain</u> to the <u>inferior olivary nucleus</u> in the medulla<br><br> | <br><br>* Ascending reticulothalamic fibers<br><br>* Descending <u>rubroolivary fibers</u><br><br>* <u>Taste</u> fibers ascending from <u>solitary nucleus</u> to the VPM <u>nucleus</u> of <u>thalamus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Coordination of movement<br><br>* Relay of <u>taste</u> fibers<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The inferior colliculi are the part of auditory pathway while the superior colliculi are the part of the visual pathway: <u>ears</u> are below the eyes.




### Blood supply of the midbrain




* <u>Tectum</u>: <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>

* <u>Tegmentum</u>

* Posterolateral part: <u>superior cerebellar artery</u>

* Posteromedial part: penetrating interpeduncular branches of the <u>basilar artery</u>

* <u>Anterior</u> part: penetrating peduncular branches of the <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>

* <u>Crura cerebri</u>

* <u>Lateral</u> parts <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>

* Middle parts penetrating peduncular branches of the <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>

* <u>Medial</u> parts <u>posterior choroidal artery</u> (arising from the <u>P2</u> segment of the <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>)





For information on the clinical relevance of the blood supply, see “<u>Midbrain syndromes</u>” in “<u>Overview of stroke</u>.”

## Pons

### Characteristics




* Location

* <u>Rostral</u> to the medulla, <u>caudal</u> to the <u>midbrain</u>

* Connected to the <u>cerebellum</u> via the <u>middle cerebellar peduncles</u>

* Function

* Conduction of nerve fibers and tracts (e.g., transmission of <u>pain</u>, temperature, <u>proprioception</u>, and auditory signals)

* Regulation of autonomic functions

* Composition: divided into 2 parts (<u>dorsal</u> to <u>ventral</u>)  

* <u>Pontine</u> <u>tegmentum</u>: contains CN <u>nuclei</u>

* <u>Trigeminal</u> (<u>CN V</u>)

* Abducens (<u>CN VI</u>)

* Facialis (<u>CN VII</u>)

* Vestibulocochlear (<u>CN VIII</u>)

* For information on the <u>cranial nerves</u>, see “<u>Cranial nerve types and functions</u>” in “<u>Cranial nerve palsies</u>.”

* Basilar <u>pons</u>: contains relay <u>nuclei</u> (e.g., <u>pontine nuclei</u>) and nerve tracts

* <u>Embryogenesis</u>: <u>rhombencephalon</u> → <u>metencephalon</u> → <u>pons</u> and <u>cerebellum</u>





### Components of the pons




| Overview of the <u>pons</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | <br>Location<br> | Components | Function |
| Cochlear nuclei | <br>* Dorsolateral aspect of the <u>pons</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ventral</u> <u>cochlear nuclei</u><br><br>* <u>Dorsal</u> <u>cochlear nuclei</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>auditory pathway</u> (second-order <u>neuron</u>)<br><br>* Receive auditory signals from the cochlear branch of the <u>vestibulocochlear nerve</u> (<u>CN VIII</u>) via special somatic afferent fibers<br><br>* Fibers project to the <u>ipsilateral</u> and <u>contralateral</u> <u>lateral lemniscus</u> via <u>acoustic striae</u><br><br><br> |
| Trapezoid body | <br><br>* <u>Ventral</u> aspect of the <u>pons</u>, <u>posterior</u> to the <u>pyramidal tracts</u><br><br>* Formed by a <u>decussation</u> of the <u>ventral</u> cochlear fibers<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Medial lemniscus</u> (see below)<br><br>* Fibers of <u>CN VI</u><br><br>* Acoustic striae: <u>axons</u> originating from the <u>cochlear nuclei</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>auditory pathway</u><br><br>* Sound localization<br><br><br> |
| Superior olivary nuclei | <br>* At the level of the <u>trapezoid body</u><br><br> | <br>* Brainstem <u>nuclei</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>auditory pathway</u> (third-order <u>neuron</u>)<br><br>* First major point of integration of auditory information from both <u>ears</u><br><br>* Relay auditory signals from the <u>cochlear nuclei</u><br><br>* Join the <u>lateral lemniscus</u> (see below) and <u>synapse</u> on the <u>neurons</u> of the <u>inferior colliculus</u> (fourth-order <u>neurons</u>).<br><br><br> |
| Corticopontine tract | <br>* Along the <u>pons</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Frontopontine fibers<br><br>* Parietopontine fibers<br><br>* Temporopontine fibers<br><br>* Occipitopontine fibers<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>corticopontocerebellar pathway</u><br><br>* <u>Synapses</u> in the <u>pontine nuclei</u><br><br><br> |
| Pontine nuclei | <br>* Basilar <u>pons</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Projection <u>neurons</u><br><br>* <u>GABAergic</u> interneurons<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>corticopontocerebellar pathway</u><br><br>* Modulation of movement<br><br>* Relay <u>cerebellar</u> signals<br><br><br> |
| Locus coeruleus | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> portion of the <u>rostral</u> <u>pons</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Melanin</u>-containing <u>nuclei</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>reticular activating system</u><br><br>* Site of <u>norepinephrine</u> production<br><br>* Projects <u>axons</u> to numerous parts of the <u>brain</u><br><br><br> |
| Medial lemniscus | <br>* <u>Medial</u> aspect of the <u>midbrain</u>, <u>pons</u>, and <u>cranial</u> medulla<br><br> | <br>* Formed by the <u>decussation</u> of internal arcuate fibers: myelinated <u>axons</u> that arise from the gracile and <u>cuneate nucleus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Pathway for <u>proprioception</u><br><br>* Transmits vibration and <u>fine touch</u><br><br>* Projects to: <u>ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus</u><br><br><br> |
| Lateral lemniscus | <br>* From <u>trapezoid body</u> to <u>nucleus</u> of <u>inferior colliculus</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Axons</u> from the <u>cochlear nuclei</u> and <u>superior olive</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>auditory pathway</u><br><br>* Projects to the <u>inferior colliculus</u><br><br><br> |
| Spinal lemniscus | <br>* Dorsolateral aspect of basilar <u>pons</u><br><br> | <br>* Ascending afferent nerve fibers<br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>spinothalamic tract</u><br><br>* <u>Nociception</u> and heat sensation<br><br><br> |





### Blood supply of the pons




* The main part of the <u>pons</u> is supplied by <u>pontine arteries</u> (penetrating branches of the <u>basilar artery</u>).

* The smaller, upper portion of the <u>pons</u> receives its blood supply from the <u>superior cerebellar artery</u> and the <u>anterior inferior cerebellar artery</u>.

* For information on the clinical relevance, see “<u>Pontine syndromes</u>” in “<u>Overview of stroke</u>.”





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Pontine stroke</u> can cause <u>ipsilateral</u> loss of function of the facial and abducens nerves with <u>contralateral</u> <u>hemiparesis</u> (<u>Millard-Gubler syndrome</u> or <u>Foville syndrome</u>).

## Medulla oblongata

### Characteristics




* Location

* <u>Rostral</u> to the spinal cord, <u>caudal</u> to the <u>pons</u>

* Connected to the <u>cerebellum</u> via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncles</u>

* Function

* Regulation of autonomic functions (e.g., circulation, respiration, gastrointestinal activity)

* Contains centers for <u>swallowing</u>, sneezing, <u>coughing</u>, and <u>vomiting</u>

* Conduction of motor and sensory information

* Composition

* CN <u>nuclei</u>

* Part of the sensory <u>trigeminal nerve</u> <u>nucleus</u> (<u>CN V</u>)

* Glossopharyngeal (<u>CN IX</u>)

* Vagus (<u>CN X</u>)

* Accessorius (<u>CN XI</u>)

* Hypoglossal (<u>CN XII</u>)

* For information on the <u>cranial nerves</u>, see “<u>Cranial nerve types and functions</u>” in “<u>Cranial nerve palsies</u>.”

* Fissures

* <u>Anterior</u> median <u>fissure</u>: extends along the entire length of the medulla

* Ventrolateral sulcus (<u>preolivary sulcus</u>)

* Separates the olives from the pyramids

* Contains rootlets of <u>CN XII</u>

* Posterolateral sulcus: contain rootlets of <u>CN IX</u>–XI

* Pyramids

* <u>Area postrema</u>

* A number of brainstem <u>nuclei</u> (e.g., <u>nucleus gracilis</u>, <u>nucleus cuneatus</u>, <u>inferior olivary nucleus</u>)

* <u>Embryogenesis</u>: <u>myelencephalon</u> → <u>medulla oblongata</u>





### Components of the medulla oblongata




| Overview of the <u>medulla oblongata</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Structure<br> | Location | Fiber tracts and course | Function |
| Gracile nucleus and cuneate nucleus | <br>* At the junction between the spinal cord and the <u>medulla oblongata</u> in the <u>dorsal column</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Contain second-order <u>neurons</u> of the <u>dorsal column</u>-<u>medial lemniscus</u> pathway<br><br>* <u>Axons</u> from these <u>neurons</u> form the <u>internal arcuate fibers</u> in the <u>pons</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Both <u>nuclei</u> relay <u>proprioception</u> and <u>fine touch</u> from first-order <u>neurons</u> located in the <u>dorsal root ganglia</u><br><br>* <u>Gracile nucleus</u>: lower trunk and legs<br><br>* <u>Cuneate nucleus</u>: upper trunk and arms<br><br> |
| Pyramids (brainstem) | <br><br>* Form the base of the medulla<br><br>* Pyramidal decussation: crossing of the fibers of the <u>corticospinal tract</u> from one side to the <u>contralateral</u> one, which occurs at the most <u>caudal</u> part of the medulla<br><br><br> | <br>* Contain the motor fibers of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts<br><br> | <br>* Voluntary motor control<br><br> |
| Accessory cuneate nucleus | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> to the <u>cuneate nucleus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Contains second-order <u>neurons</u> of the <u>cuneocerebellar tract</u><br><br>* Fibers travel to the <u>cerebellum</u> via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Proprioception</u> (upper extremities)<br><br> |
| Inferior olivary nucleus | <br>* Forms a swelling on the <u>anterior</u> surface of the <u>medulla oblongata</u>, <u>lateral</u> to both pyramids, called olivary bodies (or olives)<br><br> | <br><br>* Receives input from various sources including the <u>red nucleus</u>, <u>cerebral cortex</u>, and spinal cord<br><br>* <u>Axons</u> travel to <u>cerebellum</u> via ascending fibers in the <u>contralateral</u> <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Relays motor and sensory information to facilitate motor coordination<br><br> |
| Lateral reticular nucleus | <br>* Located at the <u>caudal</u>, ventrolateral <u>medulla oblongata</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Receives input from the spinal cord, the <u>cerebral cortex</u>, the <u>red nucleus</u>, and <u>superior colliculus</u><br><br>* Fibers travel to the <u>cerebellum</u> via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Relay <u>nucleus</u> for <u>cerebellar</u> signals<br><br>* Integration motor information<br><br>* Adjustment and regulation of motor activity<br><br><br> |
| Arcuate nucleus (medulla) | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> to the pyramids<br><br> | <br><br>* Receives input from the <u>corticospinal tract</u><br><br>* Forms the arcuatocerebellar tract of the <u>striae medullares</u> (in the rhomboid fossa)<br><br>* Fibers travel to the <u>cerebellum</u> via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Chemoreception<br><br>* Breathing control (e.g., modulation of <u>respiratory rate</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Solitary nucleus | <br>* Located within the dorsomedial medulla<br><br> | <br><br>* The solitary tract contains <u>axons</u> of the <u>cranial nerves</u> that provide input to the <u>solitary nucleus</u>:<br><br>* General <u>visceral</u> afferent signals from the glossopharyngeal (<u>CN IX</u>) and <u>vagus nerves</u> (<u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* Special <u>visceral</u> afferent signals from the facial (<u>CN VII</u>), glossopharyngeal (<u>CN IX</u>), and <u>vagus nerves</u> (<u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* Projects <u>ipsilateral</u> fibers to the posteromedial <u>nucleus</u> of the <u>thalamus</u> and the <u>pons</u> via the <u>central tegmental tract</u><br><br>* Connected to the <u>area postrema</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Relay <u>nucleus</u> for general <u>visceral</u> and <u>taste</u> afferents<br><br>* Blood pressure <u>homeostasis</u> (mediates the <u>baroreceptor reflex</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Area postrema (<u>vomiting</u> center)<br> | <br>* Located <u>anterior</u> to the <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u> on the floor of the medulla<br><br> | <br>* Receives input from the:<br><br>* <u>Nucleus tractus solitarius</u> (main coordinator)<br><br>* <u>GI tract</u> via <u>vagus nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Vestibular system</u><br><br>* <u>CNS</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Chemoreception<br><br>* Control of autonomic functions (e.g., blood pressure, appetite)<br><br>* Triggers <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Contains the chemoreceptor trigger zone, a region with no <u>blood-brain barrier</u> and, accordingly, in direct contact with the bloodstream that can trigger <u>vomiting</u> when stimulated by certain circulating substances (e.g., toxins, <u>hormones</u>)<br><br>* <u>Receptors</u> <br><br>* Muscarinic (M1)<br><br>* <u>Histamine</u> (H1)<br><br>* Neurokinin (NK–1)<br><br>* <u>Dopamine</u> (D2)<br><br>* <u>Serotonin</u> (5–HT3)<br><br>* <u>Antagonism</u> of these <u>receptors</u> is used to treat:<br><br>* <u>Chemotherapy</u>-induced <u>vomiting</u> (NK–1, D2, and 5–HT3)<br><br>* <u>Motion sickness</u> (M1 and H1)<br><br>* <u>Hyperemesis gravidarum</u> (H1)<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>gracilis muscle</u> is a muscle of the lower body, the <u>gracile nucleus</u> relays <u>fine touch</u> and <u>proprioception</u> from the lower body.




### Cross-sectional layers of the <u>medulla oblongata</u>




| Overview of cross-sectional layers in the <u>medulla oblongata</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Level (from inferior to superior) | <br><u>Anterior</u> (from <u>medial</u> to <u>lateral</u>) | <br><u>Posterior</u> (from <u>medial</u> to <u>lateral</u>) | <br><u>Lateral</u> (from <u>posterior</u> to <u>anterior</u>) | <br>Central (from <u>posterior</u> to <u>anterior</u>) |
| <u>Decussation</u> of pyramids | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> median <u>fissure</u><br><br>* Pyramids<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> median <u>fissure</u><br><br>* <u>Gracile fasciculus</u> (<u>posterior</u>) and <u>nucleus</u> (<u>anterior</u>)<br><br>* <u>Cuneate fasciculus</u> (<u>posterior</u>) and <u>nucleus</u> (<u>anterior</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Spinal <u>nucleus</u> of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u> (<u>CN V</u>)<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> <u>spinocerebellar tract</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> and <u>anterior</u> <u>spinothalamic tracts</u> (<u>spinal lemniscus</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Central canal</u><br><br>* <u>Decussation</u> of pyramids<br><br>* <u>Medial longitudinal fasciculus</u> (<u>lateral</u> to the <u>decussation</u> of pyramids)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Decussation</u> of <u>medial lemnisci</u> | <br><br>* <u>Central canal</u><br><br>* Hypoglossal <u>nucleus</u> (<u>CN XII</u>)<br><br>* <u>Medial longitudinal fasciculus</u> (<u>medial</u> to the <u>decussation</u> of <u>medial lemnisci</u>)<br><br>* <u>Internal arcuate fibers</u> (<u>decussation</u> of <u>medial lemnisci</u>)<br><br>* <u>Inferior olivary nucleus</u> (<u>lateral</u> to the <u>decussation</u> of <u>medial lemnisci</u>)<br><br><br> |  |  |  |
| <br>Olives <br> | <br><br>* <u>Pyramidal tracts</u><br><br>* <u>Hypoglossal nerve</u> (<u>CN XII</u>) rootlet<br><br>* Olivary complex<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u><br><br>* <u>Nuclei</u><br><br>* <u>Hypoglossal nerve</u> (<u>CN XII</u>)<br><br>* <u>Dorsal nucleus</u> of <u>vagus nerve</u> (<u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* <u>Solitary nucleus</u><br><br>* <u>Medial</u> and inferior <u>vestibular nuclei</u> (<u>CN VIII</u>)<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> <u>cochlear nucleus</u> (<u>CN VIII</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Inferior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> <u>cochlear nucleus</u> (<u>CN VIII</u>)<br><br>* CN rootlets:<br><br>* <u>Vagus nerve</u> (<u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* <u>Glossopharyngeal nerve</u> (<u>CN IX</u>, superior to <u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* Spinal <u>nucleus</u> of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Nucleus ambiguus</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> and <u>lateral</u> <u>spinocerebellar tracts</u><br><br><br> | <br>* From <u>posterior</u> to <u>anterior</u><br><br>* <u>Medial longitudinal fasciculus</u><br><br>* <u>Tectospinal tract</u><br><br>* <u>Medial lemniscus</u><br><br> |





### Blood supply of the medulla oblongata




* Anteromedial part: <u>anterior spinal artery</u>

* Posterolateral part

* <u>Posterior inferior cerebellar artery</u> (branch of the <u>vertebral artery</u>) at the level of the olives (<u>rostral</u> part of the medulla)

* <u>Posterior spinal artery</u> at the level of <u>pyramidal decussation</u> (<u>caudal</u> part of the medulla)

* <u>Lateral</u> part: penetrating branches of the <u>vertebral arteries</u>

* Clinical significance: <u>medullary syndromes</u>, <u>bulbar palsy</u>
